name: Nebo (the Sky-Father)

primary_sources.name: Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)
Modern comparative reconstruction (e.g., Ivanov & Toporov, 'Theses on Slavic Mythology')

description_short: In folk (and partly reconstructed) belief, 'the sky' personified as the supreme heavenly father — the highest deity, above the named gods. Whether Nebo was a formal pre-Christian god or a folk Christianization is debated.
description_long: 'Nebo' (the sky) was personified in Slavic folk belief as the supreme heavenly father — the 'sky-father' above all the named gods [S4][S5][S6]. In the folk (post-Christian) world, Nebo is the highest, a kind of supreme creator who sends the rain and the thunder [S5]. Scholars differ on whether Nebo was a formal pre-Christian deity or a folk concept that absorbed the role of the supreme sky-god (Perun) after Christianization [S6]. The name 'Nebo' itself is common across Slavic languages [S4]. We treat Nebo as the reconstructed supreme sky-father, noting that its pre-Christian status is debated [S6].
interesting_facts: The 'sky-father', the supreme deity in folk belief [S4][S5].
Whether a formal pre-Christian god or a folk Christianization is debated [S6].
uncertainty_notes: Nebo's pre-Christian status is genuinely debated: some see it as the supreme pre-Christian god, others as a folk layer that absorbed Perun's role [S6].
Do not confuse 'Nebo' (the sky-father) with 'Nebe' (a common Slavic word for 'sky/heaven' used in Christian contexts).

name: Perun

primary_sources.name: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let / Latopis povest' vremen'nykh let)
Hypatian / Hletovskaya Chronicle (Kiev idol list)
'Tale of the Destruction of the Idols' (Skazanie o razrushenii idolov)
Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)
Modern comparative reconstruction (e.g., Ivanov & Toporov, 'Theses on Slavic Mythology')

description_short: The supreme thunder-god of the pre-Christian Slavs, the sky-father, god of thunder, lightning, war, and the sacred oak. His great idol stood on a hill in Kiev, destroyed in 980 CE.
description_long: Perun is the supreme thunder-god of the pre-Christian Slavs — the sky-father, the god of thunder, lightning, war, and the sacred oak [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He was the head of the Kiev pantheon: in the Primary Chronicle, the pagan ruler Vladimir of Kiev (980 CE) erected a great wooden idol of Perun on a hill (the 'Khorivets' hill) by the Dnieper, with a golden head and beard, and a row of other gods below [S1][S3]. The 'Tale of the Destruction of the Idols' (a later retelling) describes the idol being dragged into the river and destroyed in 980 [S3]. Perun's attributes: the hammer (the weapon that hurls thunder/lightning), the sacred oak (his tree), the sacred fire (he was 'the fire-god' in some accounts — the sacred flame that was not extinguished) [S4][S5][S6]. Perun is the great antagonist of Veles (the underworld god) in the reconstructed 'Perun-Veles' conflict [S6]. Perun's role is comparable to the Indo-European sky-father (Zeus, Thor, Dyaus Pitar) [S6].
interesting_facts: The supreme thunder-god, head of the Kiev pantheon [S1][S4].
His great idol stood on a hill in Kiev, destroyed in 980 CE [S1][S3].
Attributes: the hammer, the sacred oak, the sacred fire [S4][S5].
Comparable to the Indo-European sky-father (Zeus, Thor, Dyaus Pitar) [S6].
The great antagonist of Veles in the reconstructed conflict [S6].
uncertainty_notes: Perun's 'sacred fire' role is debated: some sources say Perun was associated with the sacred flame, others attribute fire to Svarog [S4][S6].
The 'hammer' as Perun's weapon is a later (folk) association; the 980 idol is described as wooden, not with a hammer [S3].

name: Veles

primary_sources.name: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let / Latopis povest' vremen'nykh let)
Hypatian / Hletovskaya Chronicle (Kiev idol list)
Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)
Modern comparative reconstruction (e.g., Ivanov & Toporov, 'Theses on Slavic Mythology')

description_short: The god of the underworld, cattle, magic, and the serpent; son of Svarog; the great antagonist of Perun. His domain is the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd).
description_long: Veles (Volos, Velas) is the god of the underworld, cattle, magic, and the serpent [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He is the son of Svarog (the sky-father/craftsman god) [S6]. Veles's domain is the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd) — the underworld — and the earth [S6]. He is the god of cattle (the 'cattle-god'), of wealth, of magic, and of the serpent (his animal) [S4][S5][S6]. The snake is a sacred symbol of Veles: the 'Veles-day' (May 22, later the feast of St. Nicholas) was associated with the awakening of the snakes (the 'Veles' snakes') and was a day of special taboos [S5]. Veles is the great antagonist of Perun in the reconstructed 'Perun-Veles' conflict: the sky-thunder-god vs. the underworld-serpent-god [S6]. This is a genuine reconstructed duality, not a single attested myth — we present it as a scholarly reconstruction [S6].
interesting_facts: God of the underworld, cattle, magic, and the serpent [S4][S5][S6].
Son of Svarog [S6].
The 'Veles-day' (May 22) was associated with the awakening of the snakes [S5].
The great antagonist of Perun (reconstructed duality) [S6].
uncertainty_notes: The 'Perun-Veles' conflict is a scholarly reconstruction (Ivanov & Toporov), not a single attested myth [S6].
Veles's 'underworld' role is reconstructed from folk belief and comparative evidence; the earliest sources do not describe his realm in detail [S6].

name: Svarog (Svarozhich)

primary_sources.name: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let / Latopis povest' vremen'nykh let)
Hypatian / Hletovskaya Chronicle (Kiev idol list)
Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)
Modern comparative reconstruction (e.g., Ivanov & Toporov, 'Theses on Slavic Mythology')

description_short: The god of fire, smithing, and crafts; father of Veles; in some accounts a sky/sun god. His name is the root of 'Svarozhich' (the 'Svarog-son').
description_long: Svarog (Svarozhich) is the god of fire, smithing, and crafts [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He is the father of Veles [S6]. In some accounts, Svarog is a sky/sun god (the 'heavenly' father), while in others he is the 'earthly' craftsman-god who works in the forge [S4][S6]. His name is the root of 'Svarozhich' ('the Svarog-son') — a name applied to the smith, the craftsman, and (in one folk account) to the ruler himself (the 'Svarozhich' as a royal title) [S5]. Svarog's fire is the forge-fire: the sacred, creative fire that shapes metal [S4][S5]. He is a patron of the smiths and the craftsmen [S5]. The relationship between Svarog and Perun's 'sacred fire' is debated: some attribute the sacred fire to Svarog, others to Perun [S4][S6].
interesting_facts: God of fire, smithing, and crafts [S4][S5].
Father of Veles [S6].
The root of the name 'Svarozhich' [S5].
The sacred forge-fire [S4][S5].
uncertainty_notes: Svarog's 'sky/sun' role vs. his 'craftsman' role are not clearly distinguished in the sources; both are attested [S4][S6].
The 'Svarozhich' as a royal title is a folk/late development [S5].

name: Dazhbog
domains: the giver of light (his name means 'day-god' or 'light-god')

primary_sources.name: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let / Latopis povest' vremen'nykh let)
Hypatian / Hletovskaya Chronicle (Kiev idol list)

description_short: The 'day-god' or 'light-god' (his name means 'giving day' or 'giving light'); a sun god, in the Kiev pantheon.
description_long: Dazhbog (Dazh'bozh) is the 'day-god' or 'light-god' — his name is generally interpreted as 'giving day' or 'giving light' (from 'dazh' = day, 'bog' = god) [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He is a sun/light god in the Kiev pantheon [S1][S2]. His exact role is less well-attested than Perun or Veles: the sources name him but give little detail [S4]. He is sometimes identified with the sun, sometimes with the daylight in general [S4][S6]. A solar cult (the 'Dazhbog' sun-worship) is attested in folk survivals [S5].
interesting_facts: The 'day-god' or 'light-god' (name = 'giving day/light') [S1][S4].
A sun/light god in the Kiev pantheon [S1][S2].
Less well-attested than Perun or Veles [S4].
uncertainty_notes: Dazhbog's exact role is poorly attested: the sources name him but give little detail [S4].
Whether 'Dazhbog' is a sun-god or a 'daylight' god is debated [S4][S6].

name: Khors
symbols: the chariot (the sun's chariot, in some accounts)

description_short: A solar god (a 'sun' deity) in the Kiev pantheon; less well-attested than Dazhbog.
description_long: Khors (Kors) is a solar god in the Kiev pantheon [S1][S2]. His exact relationship to Dazhbog (the 'day-god') is unclear: the two are both solar/light deities, and their distinction is not well-defined in the sources [S4]. Khors is named in the idol list but given little detail [S4]. Some scholars see Khors as a 'solar' god and Dazhbog as a 'daylight' god; others see them as overlapping [S6].
interesting_facts: A solar god in the Kiev pantheon [S1][S2].
Less well-attested than Dazhbog [S4].
uncertainty_notes: The distinction between Khors and Dazhbog is not clear in the sources [S4][S6].

name: Stribog

description_short: The god of the wind, the air, the breath of the sky; in the Kiev pantheon. The 'Stribog' is the wind itself in folk belief.
description_long: Stribog is the god of the wind, the air, the breath of the sky [S1][S2][S4][S5]. In the Primary Chronicle, Stribog is named as the 'father of the winds' (he 'sends the winds') [S1]. In folk belief, the 'Stribog' is the wind itself, and the wind is sometimes personified as a deity [S5]. Stribog's role is clear (the wind-god) but his mythic biography is not attested [S4].
interesting_facts: God of the wind, the air [S1][S2][S4].
'The father of the winds' in the Primary Chronicle [S1].
The wind itself, personified, in folk belief [S5].
uncertainty_notes: Stribog's mythic biography is not attested; the sources name him as the wind-god but give no stories [S4].

name: Mokosh

primary_sources.name: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let / Latopis povest' vremen'nykh let)

description_short: The goddess of fertility, the earth, weaving, and the fate (the spinning of destiny); in the Kiev pantheon. Her name is the root of the common Slavic word for 'moisture/wetness'.
description_long: Mokosh (Mocoš) is the goddess of fertility, the earth, weaving, and the fate (the spinning of destiny) [S1][S2][S4][S5]. Her name is generally interpreted as related to the common Slavic word for 'moisture/wetness' (the life-giving wetness of the earth) [S4]. Mokosh is the patroness of women's work (weaving, spinning) and of the fate — the 'spinning of destiny' (the threads of life) [S5]. In folk belief, the 'Mokosh' is associated with the earth-mother, the fertility of the land, and the fate of the household [S5]. She is named in the Kiev idol list [S1][S2]. Her relationship to the 'fate-spinning' (the Moirai/Norns equivalent) is a reconstructed parallel [S6].
interesting_facts: Goddess of fertility, the earth, weaving, and the fate [S4][S5].
Name related to the Slavic word for 'moisture/wetness' [S4].
The 'spinning of destiny' (the fate) [S5][S6].
uncertainty_notes: Mokosh's 'fate-spinning' role is a reconstructed parallel to the Moirai/Norns, not a single attested myth [S6].

name: Lada

primary_sources.name: Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)

description_short: The goddess of spring, fertility, beauty, and the household; in folk belief the 'Lada' is the beloved, the beautiful one. Her status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated.
description_long: Lada is the goddess of spring, fertility, beauty, and the household [S4][S5]. In folk belief, the 'Lada' is the beloved, the beautiful one (the word 'lada' means 'beautiful, lovely, harmonious') [S5]. Lada is associated with the spring, the blossoming, the fertility of the land, and the harmony of the household [S4][S5]. Her status as a formal pre-Christian goddess (vs. a folk concept) is debated: the 'Lada' is more clearly a folk deity than a member of the formal Kiev pantheon [S6]. She is a 'spring/fertility' goddess, comparable to the Indo-European spring-maidens [S6].
interesting_facts: Goddess of spring, fertility, beauty, and the household [S4][S5].
The 'Lada' = the beloved, the beautiful one [S5].
More clearly a folk deity than a formal pantheon member [S6].
uncertainty_notes: Lada's status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated; she is more clearly a folk concept [S6].

name: Morana (Marena)

primary_sources.name: Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)

description_short: The goddess of death and winter; in folk tradition the 'drowning of Marzanna' (an effigy of the winter-goddess) is a spring-ritual that 'kills' winter and 'calls' spring. Her pre-Christian status is debated.
description_long: Morana (Marena, Morena) is the goddess of death and winter [S4][S5]. In folk tradition, the 'drowning of Marzanna' (the 'Marzanna'/'Morana' doll) is a spring-ritual: an effigy of the winter-goddess is made, carried around, and drowned in a river to 'kill' winter and 'call' spring [S5]. This is a well-attested folk ritual (the 'proshchanie s zimoi' = 'farewell to winter') [S5]. Morana's status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated: the 'Marzanna'/'Morana' is more clearly a folk death/winter figure than a member of the formal Kiev pantheon [S6]. She is the great antagonist of Jarilo (the spring/youth god) in the reconstructed seasonal cycle [S6].
interesting_facts: Goddess of death and winter [S4][S5].
The 'drowning of Marzanna' is a well-attested folk spring-ritual [S5].
The great antagonist of Jarilo (reconstructed seasonal cycle) [S6].
uncertainty_notes: Morana's status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated; she is more clearly a folk death/winter figure [S6].
The 'Marzanna'/'Morana'/'Marena' are regional variants of the same winter/death figure [S5].

name: Jarilo (Kupala)

primary_sources.name: Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)
Modern comparative reconstruction (e.g., Ivanov & Toporov, 'Theses on Slavic Mythology')

description_short: The god of spring, youth, and the sun; in folk tradition the 'Kupala' night (the midsummer solstice) is a fire-and-water festival. His relationship to the 'Kupala' ritual is well-attested in folk tradition.
description_long: Jarilo (Yarilo) is the god of spring, youth, and the sun [S4][S5]. In folk tradition, the 'Kupala' night (the midsummer solstice, around June 23/24) is a fire-and-water festival: bonfires are lit, people leap over the fire, and the 'Kupala' flower (the fern-flower) is sought [S5]. The 'Kupala' ritual is well-attested in folk tradition across Slavic lands [S5]. Jarilo's relationship to the 'Kupala' festival is debated: some see Jarilo as the 'Kupala' god (the spring/youth/sun god), others see the 'Kupala' as a separate (possibly older) water/sun ritual [S6]. Jarilo is the great antagonist of Morana (the winter/death goddess) in the reconstructed seasonal cycle [S6].
interesting_facts: God of spring, youth, and the sun [S4][S5].
The 'Kupala' night (midsummer) is a well-attested folk fire-and-water festival [S5].
The great antagonist of Morana (reconstructed seasonal cycle) [S6].
uncertainty_notes: The relationship between Jarilo and the 'Kupala' festival is debated: is Jarilo the 'Kupala' god, or is the 'Kupala' a separate older ritual? [S6].
Jarilo's 'sun' role is debated; in some accounts he is the 'spring' god, in others the 'sun' god [S4][S6].

name: Zorya (the Morning Stars)

primary_sources.name: Vsevolod Miller, 'Slavic God-Concepts' (Slavjanskije bozhestvennye predstavl'enija)
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)
Modern comparative reconstruction (e.g., Ivanov & Toporov, 'Theses on Slavic Mythology')

description_short: The goddess (or pair of goddesses) of the dawn and the morning star (Venus); the 'Zorya' is the 'gate' of the sky, the threshold between the human world and the divine. In folk belief the 'Zorya' is the 'guardian of the threshold'.
description_long: Zorya (Zarja) is the goddess (or pair of goddesses) of the dawn and the morning star (Venus) [S4][S5]. The 'Zorya' is the 'gate' of the sky, the threshold between the human world and the divine [S5]. In folk belief, the 'Zorya' is the 'guardian of the threshold' — she opens and closes the 'gate of the sky' (the dawn) [S5]. There are two 'Zorya': the 'Zorya Voshodnyaya' (the Rising Star, the dawn) and the 'Zorya Zakatnaya' (the Setting Star, the dusk) [S5]. The 'Zorya' is a well-attested folk figure (the dawn, the morning star), though her status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated [S6].
interesting_facts: Goddess of the dawn and the morning star (Venus) [S4][S5].
The 'gate' of the sky, the threshold [S5].
The 'guardian of the threshold' in folk belief [S5].
uncertainty_notes: Zorya's status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated; she is more clearly a folk dawn/star figure [S6].
The 'two Zorya' (rising and setting) are a folk elaboration [S5].

name: Cherd (Chert)

primary_sources.name: Modern comparative reconstruction (e.g., Ivanov & Toporov, 'Theses on Slavic Mythology')
19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)

description_short: The god of the underworld, the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd); in folk (post-Christian) belief the 'Chert' (the devil) is a Christianization of the underworld-god. His pre-Christian status is debated.
description_long: 'Cherd' (Chert) is the reconstructed god of the underworld, the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd) [S6]. In folk (post-Christian) belief, the 'Chert' (the devil) is often seen as a Christianization of the pre-Christian underworld-god [S6]. The 'Cherd'/'Chert' is the lord of the underworld, the realm of the dead [S6]. His pre-Christian status is debated: the 'Chert' is more clearly a folk/Christian figure than a formal pre-Christian deity [S6]. We present Cherd as the reconstructed underworld-god, noting that his pre-Christian identity is uncertain [S6].
interesting_facts: The reconstructed god of the underworld, the realm of the dead [S6].
The 'Chert' (the devil) is a Christianization of the underworld-god [S6].
uncertainty_notes: Cherd's pre-Christian status is debated; the 'Chert' is more clearly a folk/Christian figure [S6].
Do not confuse the pre-Christian underworld-god with the Christian 'devil' — they are distinct, though the folk tradition merged them [S6].
